visual.text: The sea keeps returning what we throw away. This Sunday, help us take it back.
Changi Beach clean-up · Sunday, 7.30 am · all hands welcome
A girl of about fourteen holds up a single faded slipper tangled in fishing line. Behind her, volunteers with tongs and sacks spread out across the sand at sunrise.

Last month we found bottles, straws, slippers and even a rice cooker — all before breakfast. None of it belongs on a beach where children dig and crabs make their homes. You do not need to be fit or know anything about the sea. If you can bend down and pick something up, you are qualified.

You bring: a water bottle, a hat and covered shoes
Afterwards: teh and curry puffs on us

questions.text: ‘If you can bend down and pick something up, you are qualified.’ What is the writer suggesting about the clean-up?

scheme.answer: Anyone can take part because the work is simple and needs no special skill, fitness or knowledge.
accept: The clean-up is easy enough for everybody, so nobody should think they are not good enough to join.

The clean-up is very tiring because you have to keep bending down.

accept: He enjoyed it and was curious to see what else he could find.

questions.text: Look at the first sentence of the headline: ‘The sea keeps returning what we throw away.’ What does it suggest about where the rubbish on the beach comes from?

scheme.answer: The rubbish was thrown away by people, and the sea washes it back onto the shore.
accept: The litter on the beach is our own; humans are responsible for it.

seeds.text: It suggests the rubbish comes from people who threw it away, and the waves wash it back up onto the beach.
The mess is caused by humans. Our own litter ends up in the water and then lands on the shore again.
